content.content:
# FirstRun ### Docs that work. Literally. FirstRun runs your quickstart in a clean container, finds the first step that breaks, and proves the fix with a second clean run. [![Live site](https://img.shields.io/badge/site-firstrun.atharvashah.com-0A66D6?style=for-the-badge)](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/) [![neatHack 2026](https://img.shields.io/badge/built%20for-%23neatHack%202026-111111?style=for-the-badge)](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) [![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-295%20offline-1B8A3A?style=for-the-badge)](.github) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.11%2B-3776AB?style=for-the-badge&logo=python&logoColor=white)](pyproject.toml) [**Watch the 3-minute demo**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JJNWWhSV9pc) · [**Try it in the browser**](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/) · [**Watch a real run**](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/run.html) · [**See the 4 upstream PRs**](#firstrun-found-4-real-docs-bugs-and-opened-4-upstream-prs) · [**Follow the build on X**](https://x.com/cultist_dev)
The 44-second launch film. The video does not play for you? [Open it on the site](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/) or [download the MP4](docs/assets/firstrun-launch.mp4).

```bash pip install git+https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun firstrun https://docs.example.com/quickstart ``` ## Break, Fix, Prove Takes 195 Seconds

1. Read
FirstRun reads the page and plans one step per command.
2. Run
Every step runs in a clean container, like a new developer. The first failure stops the run.
3. Prove
A fix is done only when a second clean container passes the whole quickstart.
The input below is a known-broken test fixture (`tests/fixtures/docs/broken_quickstart_FIXTURE.md`), not a real project's docs. Step 3 pins an old chromadb that cannot install on Python 3.11. ```text Step 3 of 4: pip install chromadb==0.3 ERROR: No matching distribution found for numpy~=1.21.6 Cause: docs_bug (source: jev) Patch: step 3 -> pip install chromadb Verified: 4/4 steps passed in a fresh container Time to first success: 195 s ``` FirstRun writes `report.md`, `patch.diff` and `pr_body.md` into the run folder. The patch is one line. ## Seven Teams Get a Different Job Out of the Same Engine | # | You are | The problem | Run this | You get | |---|---|---|---|---| | **1** | A DevRel or docs lead | Nobody tests the quickstart after launch day | `firstrun ` | A pass or a verified fix, with a PR draft | | **2** | A release manager | A new release of your package broke the docs and you do not know which one | `firstrun bisect --package ` | The last good and first bad release | | **3** | A technical writer | The docs assume tools the reader does not have | `firstrun prereqs ` | A Prerequisites block, proven in a clean container | | **4** | An open-source contributor | You want a first PR that a maintainer merges | `firstrun pr ` | The `gh` commands for the docs PR, source check included | | **5** | An engineer picking a tool | You want to know if the vendor's quickstart works before you commit | `firstrun ` | A time to first success and the first step that breaks | | **6** | A coding agent | You need a loop that checks its own docs work | `firstrun run --resume ` | State after every step and a model-free verify | | **7** | A head of docs | Hundreds of pages, and the code moved under some of them | `firstrun audit owner/repo` | Stale pages with the commits behind them, features with no docs, proposal cards and drafted release notes |
7. Which docs did the product outgrow? Audit the whole docs set from the git history. ```bash firstrun audit fastapi/typer ``` ```bash firstrun audit dbt-labs/dbt-core --docs-repo dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com ``` One blobless clone gives the whole history. The audit then works offline and costs $0 in model calls. Jev sorts commits with no conventional prefix when `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` is set, and every audit is one neatlogs trace. - **Oldest first.** Every page, ranked by the date of its last edit. - **Stale or quiet.** A page is stale when product commits on its topic landed after its last edit, and the report names those commits. An old page that nothing changed under is quiet, so the team can leave it alone. - **Features with no docs.** Each user-facing commit in 120 days is checked against the docs text. A flag or name that no page mentions becomes a "Document this" card. - **Proposal cards.** Document this, refresh this page, feature this, create content around a feature with 3 or more commits, and automate the release notes. - **Drafts.** Release notes for the newest stable tag and up to 3 product highlights, written from commit subjects and pull request numbers. `firstrun audit-issue` turns the newest audit into `issue.md`, one checkbox per card, and prints the `gh issue create` command. It opens nothing on its own. To audit every week, copy [`examples/github-action/firstrun-audit.yml`](examples/github-action/firstrun-audit.yml) into `.github/workflows/`. Each Monday it audits the repo and updates one issue labeled `firstrun-audit`, so the docs team gets a fresh work list without anyone running a command. `--docs-repo` reads the docs from a second repo when the docs site lives apart from the code. Inside this repo, each audit is published to `docs/audits/` and opens at [audit.html](https://1run.netlify.app/audit.html).
1. Does my quickstart work today? Run it every night.
A DevRel team ships a quickstart once and a dependency moves the week after. The first person to find the break is a new user, and most new users leave instead of filing a bug. ```bash firstrun https://docs.example.com/quickstart ``` A clean pass ends as `passed`. A break ends as `verified` once a second container proves the fix. The nightly check costs $0.0167 per run on average over 64 runs, measured by neatlogs at list price.
2. Which release broke it, and when? Docs Bisect names the package version.
```bash firstrun bisect --package jafgen ``` FirstRun binary-searches the package's releases, one fresh container per probe, with the version pinned through `PIP_CONSTRAINT`. It replays stored commands, so a bisect makes no model calls. **Real result:** the dbt DuckDB guide never worked in a clean environment. Its step `jafgen --years 6` passes on jafgen 0.3.1 (2023-01-17) and fails on 0.4.6 (2024-04-07). PyPI has no release between them. The guide merged on 2025-03-14, 11 months after `--years` was gone. 5 probes found it.
3. What does it silently assume? Prerequisite Proof writes the missing block.
```bash firstrun prereqs ``` FirstRun turns the container fixes of a run into a Prerequisites block. Then it proves the block. A fresh container with only those items runs the docs as written. | Quickstart | The docs assume | Proof in a clean `python:3.11-slim` | |---|---|---| | AccuKnox knoxctl | curl, ca-certificates, gnupg, sudo | proven, 5/5 steps | | MkDocs | curl | proven, 9/9 steps | | Entire install | curl, git, `~/.local/bin` on `PATH` | proven, 4/4 steps, git found in round 2 | | dbt + DuckDB | Python 3.12 or later, git | steps 1 to 9 pass on `python:3.12-slim`, step 10 is the jafgen docs bug |
4. Open the docs PR. A verified fix becomes an upstream pull request.
```bash firstrun pr ``` FirstRun prints the `gh` commands and a PR body. Every draft gets a source check first, because a docs note can look like a docs bug. FirstRun opened 4 real PRs this way. They are listed [below](#firstrun-found-4-real-docs-bugs-and-opened-4-upstream-prs).
5. Test a vendor before you adopt it. Time to first success is the number.
Point FirstRun at any public quickstart. The report shows how long a new developer needs to reach a working result, and where they get stuck first.
6. Give your coding agent the loop. Plan, run, recover, verify, with a trace.
The site hands you a prompt for Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. The agent installs FirstRun, checks Docker, runs your quickstart, proves the fix and opens the PR when you say yes. `state.json` is written after every step, so a run resumes with `firstrun run --resume RUN_ID`.
## Radar Picks the Quickstarts Worth a Run, and the Run Log Picks the Buyers FirstRun spends model money on every run, so it should only run where a break is likely and someone will read the fix. 1. **Find.** Exa search returns candidate quickstart pages at no cost. 2. **Rank.** `scripts/radar.py` asks Jev 4 typed questions per page in one call: can it run unattended in a container, is a step likely to break, how many developers read it, and is it the official docs. Code multiplies the answers into one priority. No model reads the pages one by one. 3. **Run.** `firstrun run --targets targets-radar.txt --tag radar --tier team` runs the top pages in 3 parallel lanes under the plan-set cost cap. Every run is logged on the [runs page](https://1run.netlify.app/runs/). 4. **Sell.** `scripts/buyers.py` maps each docs site FirstRun ran on or audited to its company, enriches it through treg at $0.0018 a lookup, and asks Jev whether the company fits the $49 to $299 plan. The result is [business/buyers.md](business/buyers.md): companies FirstRun already has proof for, each linked to its replay. # neatHack Build Log: FirstRun

## Project

- **Name:** FirstRun
- **Purpose:** FirstRun runs your quickstart in a clean container, finds the first step that breaks, and proves the fix with a second clean run.
- **Problem:** Quickstarts break when a package is renamed, a flag is removed or a version moves. Nobody on the team gets an alert. The first person who finds the break is a new user, and most new users leave.

## Team

- Atharva Shah ([@HighnessAtharva](https://github.com/HighnessAtharva)), solo.

## Stack

| Part | Tool |
|---|---|
| Language | Python 3.11 |
| Agent | Claude Agent SDK, model `claude-sonnet-5-5` at medium effort, auth through `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` |
| Tracing | neatlogs Python SDK 1.4.26, neatlogs CLI 0.2.0 |
| Sandbox | Docker Engine 29.8.2 in WSL Ubuntu 22.04, one fresh container per run |
| Docs reader | Firecrawl CLI 1.25.3 |
| Failure classifier | Jev (TypeSafe System One) |
| Session capture | Entire CLI 0.11.4: Checkpoints, Graph, Brain, Trails |
| Business plan | cfo.ai |

## Planning Happened Before the Event

one job. No FirstRun code existed before kickoff on 2026-10-10 at 12:30 PM IST.

neatlogs

Traces every run.
The planner, executor and verifier show up as spans, so a bad run has a cause you can read.

Entire

Records every session.
Each agent commit carries the Claude Code session that wrote it, so its lines trace to a prompt.

cfo.ai

Turns cost into a plan.
The measured cost per run from neatlogs goes into the pricing model.
### neatlogs Shows What the Agent Did Each run is one `firstrun.run` trace. The span kinds are WORKFLOW, AGENT, TOOL and GUARDRAIL. Claude calls appear as typed LLM spans.

One trace per run. Reading, planning, every step and verification sit under one root span.
A custom detection. "Docs step broke" flags failed tool spans. 40 flagged.

Detection analysis. 132 traces, 154 errors. "Docs step broke" hit 35 times, 12.9%.
Investigate. A 52.8x spike in Execution Failed opened a root cause with a confidence score.

Recovery spans. Classify, search, patch and retry show as `recover.N` spans.
Analytics. 132 traces and $0.9071 total cost, in one view.
Two detections run on the traces: "docs step broke" and "planner invented a step". The second one flagged 3 planner spans in v1. Investigate traced them to the planner prompt and proposed a stricter one ([evidence/neatlogs-investigation.md](evidence/neatlogs-investigation.md)). A Claude Code session read the detection and its trend over the neatlogs MCP server and applied the fix in commit 3ca6f11. The fix adds code guards that drop invented, placeholder and fake-secret steps. The integration check read 3 real runs back from persisted traces. See [docs/neatlogs-integration.md](docs/neatlogs-integration.md). ### Entire Records How the Build Happened

A checkpoint on each agent commit. The commit maps back to the session that wrote it.
A merge gate. The merge stays blocked while a high finding is open.
Inline review. The finding sits on the line in src/firstrun/recovery.py.
- **Checkpoints:** 74 of 88 normal commits carry an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer, counted with `git log` on 2026-10-11. The 4 setup commits before the first agent session and 10 site commits carry none. Merge commits carry none, because Entire's hook skips merges. The neatlogs fix commit shows the full agent session behind it: [checkpoint 01M4JGJ6NTE7YNB9Z0YW5FYVHN](https://entire.io/gh/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/commit/3ca6f118ecb0a8915315eea27b5588dd8a7c6299). - **Trail reviews:** Entire runners reviewed every layer on Trails 3 to 7. They raised 2 real bugs on Layer 1, a secret retry loop and a Windows-only Docker default, both fixed in e2aacb7. - **Trails:** [Trail 1](https://entire.io/gh/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/trails/1) covers Layer 1. Trail pages need an entire.io login. The commit and session pages open without one. - **Graph:** the build agents searched the repo through the graph. 4 graph calls saved about 11,662 tokens. - **Brain:** it holds 7 durable facts, such as why recovery stops at 3 attempts. Its last refresh indexed 63 files and 1,056 symbols. ### cfo.ai Prices the Nightly Check

Ari, the cfo.ai agent, on day one.		 The business plan sets the agent's spending limit. `firstrun econ` reads 88 neatlogs traces and writes [business/drivers.csv](business/drivers.csv) for cfo.ai. The mean run costs $0.0178, and the p95 run costs $0.0529. A 70% margin floor turns those costs into a cap per tier, and `firstrun run --tier scale` stops any run that spends past the cap. | Tier | Price | Quickstarts | Cap per run | Runs over the cap | |---|---|---|---|---| | Free | $0 | 1, weekly | $0.0135 | 50.0% | | Team | $49 a month | 10, nightly | $0.0470 | 9.1% | | Scale | $299 a month | 100, nightly, with PRs, Bisect and Prerequisite Proof | $0.0279 | 26.1% | The old fixed cap of $0.50 let one bad month cost a Scale customer's fee five times over. The plan, the Scale fix and every assumption are in [business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md](business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md). The cfo.ai model is public at [https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE). Under the old cap, cash goes negative in month 14. The [plan page](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/plan/) shows the caps, the measured cost spread and the cash per Scenario. Every doc-test run is tagged against the caps. A neatlogs alert uses the Scale cap as its threshold, and `scripts/neatlogs_issues.py` mirrors each detection and alert as a GitHub issue labeled [`neatlogs`](https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/issues?q=label%3Aneatlogs).

## Run Your First Check in 5 Minutes You need: - Python 3.11 or newer. - Git. `pip install git+https://...` clones the repo, so it fails without git. - Docker. On Windows, run Docker inside WSL with the `Ubuntu-22.04` distro. - A Claude subscription token in `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`. Create one with `claude setup-token`. - Optional: `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` for traces. - Optional: `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` for Jev. Without it, Claude classifies the failure. Install: ```bash pip install git+https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun ``` FirstRun reads keys from `.env` in the folder you run it from. To use another file, set `FIRSTRUN_ENV_FILE`: ```bash export FIRSTRUN_ENV_FILE=/path/to/your/.env ``` FirstRun uses `docker` from your `PATH`. On Windows without it, FirstRun calls Docker inside WSL with `wsl -d Ubuntu-22.04 docker`. Set `FIRSTRUN_DOCKER` to use another command. Run it on a quickstart URL: ```bash firstrun https://docs.example.com/quickstart ``` A URL tested in the last 24 hours returns the cached result. Add `--fresh` to run it again. Read the result in `runs//report.md`. Build the HTML report with: ```bash firstrun report --html ``` Run it inside a clone of this repo and every run is logged for the public site. FirstRun writes the replay to `docs/runs/` and adds a row to `docs/runs/index.json`. Commit those files and the run appears on the [runs page](https://1run.netlify.app/runs/). Rebuild the log from the `runs/` folder with: ```bash firstrun publish --all ``` The offline test suite needs no network, Docker or keys. The tests ship with the repo, not with the pip package, so clone it first: ```bash git clone https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun ``` ```bash cd firstrun && pip install -e ".[dev]" && pytest -q ``` FirstRun ran this section on itself in a clean `python:3.11-slim` container. The install failed until git was present, which is why git is listed above. The run step then stopped with the missing-token message, because a clean container has no Claude token or Docker. ## One Trace Follows the Docs Page From Read to Verified Fix ```mermaid flowchart TD A[docs URL] --> B["read_docs
Firecrawl · TOOL"] B --> C["planner

new container, no model calls · GUARDRAIL"] --> K["report.md

pr_body.md"] ``` A `budget` GUARDRAIL span runs before every recovery. The root span `firstrun.run` is a WORKFLOW span that holds the whole tree. [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) lists the states, the failure classes, the budgets and every span. ## Each of the 8 Focus Areas Has a Feature You Can Open | Focus area | Feature | Where you see it | |---|---|---| | Planning | The planner turns the docs page into a runbook | `runbook.json`, the `planner` span | | Tool use | Firecrawl reads, Docker runs, Jev classifies | One TOOL span per call | | State | `state.json` is written after every step | `firstrun run --resume RUN_ID` | | Context | The planner reads only the quickstart page | `read_docs` span input | | Execution | One fresh container per run | `step.N` spans with exit codes | | Recovery | Classify, search, patch, retry up to 3 times | `recover.N` span | | Verification | A model-free re-run in a new container | `verify` span, status `verified` | | Iteration | v1 traces, detections, a fix, v2 traces | The results table below | ## Version 2 Finishes 3 of 4 Quickstarts and Recovers 3 Failed Steps v1 ran with recovery off. v2 ran after the neatlogs planner fix (3ca6f11), with recovery and verification on. The same four targets ran both times. Cost and duration come from the neatlogs traces in [evidence/before_after_traces.json](evidence/before_after_traces.json). The six mistakes the agent made in v1: 1. The plan changes between runs. The same neatlogs page gave 4 steps, then 3 steps, 5 minutes later. 2. The planner invents steps. It added `command -v entire` and `test -f first_trace.py`, which the docs never say. 3. The planner writes placeholder steps. Chroma step 2 is `true`. 4. Every PR draft gets a source check before it ships. - **A cd broke steps three ways.** A leading cd, a cd inside a patched chain, and a file check after cd each failed a step that worked. The container now treats a cd into the folder it is already in as a no-op, and file checks also look from the run root. - **The Entire Brain watcher does not run on Windows.** Brain runs with `--no-daemon` and is refreshed by hand. # FirstRun Business Plan

FirstRun runs a dev tool's quickstart in a clean container every night, finds the first step that breaks, proves the fix with a second clean run, and drafts the docs PR. The buyer is a DevRel or docs team at a dev-tool company.

The business plan sets the agent's spending limit. `firstrun econ` reads every neatlogs trace, cfo.ai turns the costs into a per-tier cap, and `firstrun run --tier` stops any run that spends past it.

cfo.ai model, public and read-only: [https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE)

## Three Tiers Price by Quickstarts Covered

| Tier | Price per month | Quickstarts | Runs per month |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 1, weekly | 4 |
| Team | $49 | 10, nightly | 300 |
| Scale | $299 | 100, nightly, with PRs, Docs Bisect and Prerequisite Proof | 3,000 |

neatlogs holds 64 `firstrun.run` traces from 2026-10-10. `firstrun econ` reads them and writes [`drivers.csv`](drivers.csv), the file cfo.ai imports. Each quantile row names the trace it came from, so a judge can open the trace behind any cost in the model.

| Driver | Cost per run | neatlogs trace |
|---|---|---|
| Mean | $0.01672 | all 64 |
| p50 | $0.01076 | `cef9cc00bcc5369d74ffc7fc5f525244` |
| p90 | $0.04424 | `ec246a27f83c9e11d682eb09a1818f58` |

The costs are Sonnet 5.5 list price, and Anthropic did not bill them. The 64 traces include 28 development runs, so the spread is wider than a production month would show.

The expensive runs are the useful ones. A run that hits a broken step pays for recovery and for the second clean run. Of 19 real-world runs, 10 ended `verified` with 32 proven patches, and the 19 runs cost $0.97 in total. That is $0.0975 per verified quickstart (source: `runs/*/state.json`).

## The Old $0.50 Cap Let a Scale Customer Cost Five Times the Price

Before this plan, every run had the same cap of $0.50 in `src/firstrun/models.py`. That cap was 30 times the mean run cost, and nothing in the business set it.

| Tier | Revenue per run | Margin at mean cost | Margin at p95 cost | Margin if every run hits $0.50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Team | $0.1633 | 88.6% | 67.7% | -207.3% |
| Scale | $0.0997 | 81.3% | 47.1% | -403.6% |

The mean says both tiers are healthy. The p95 says Scale falls below a 70% margin in a month with many broken quickstarts. The old cap says one bad month can cost a Scale customer's fee five times over.

## The Margin Floor Sets the Cap, and the Agent Enforces It

The founder picks one number, a 70% gross margin floor. The cap for each tier is the model spend one run may use and still keep that floor:

```text
cap per run = price / runs per month x (1 - margin floor) - compute per run
```

# Verbatim

### If we didn't fetch it, we didn't say it.

A research agent where **every sentence carries a receipt**. Each claim is checked
by a deterministic verifier that did not write it: the verifier re-reads the cited
source and confirms the quoted evidence is actually in it. Claims that fail are
struck and re-researched. Claims that cannot be verified are named as unverified
instead of being asserted.

Built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) · Oct 10–12 2026 · solo.

---

## The problem, in one paragraph

Agents now self-certify. The evidence that this is broken is unambiguous and
recent:

- **Rao, Wong & Callison-Burch** (arXiv 2604.03173) measured **3–13% of citation
  URLs that likely never existed** across 53,090 and 168,021 citations, and found
  deep research agents hallucinate at *higher* rates than plain search-augmented
  LLMs — the deeper they research, the worse it gets.
- **SciConBench** (arXiv 2606.11337) puts the best deep-research agent at a
  factual **F1 of 0.337** under clean-room evaluation, and finds consumer agents
  producing contradictory conclusions even with ground truth available.
- **OpenAI** retired SWE-bench Verified in February 2026 after finding **59.4% of
  audited tasks had tests that reject correct solutions**, and that every frontier
  model could reproduce the gold patch verbatim.

Every one of those failures is a *verification* failure. An agent that grades its
own work is not measuring its own work.

## The idea

Verbatim inverts the pipeline. The step that decides whether the agent is right
contains **no language model at all**:

```
plan → retrieve → claim → VERIFY → repair → compile
                              ↑
                    five deterministic checks,
                    no LLM in any of them
```

The check that has no equivalent anywhere else is **prior leak**: if a claim's
distinctive facts appear in *no* source we actually fetched, it came from the
model's memory rather than from this run — and it cannot ship, **even when it
happens to be true**. Truth is not the standard. Evidence is.

### The five checks

| # | Check | Catches | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Source available** — the cited source was fetched and is not dead | unreadable links | `unverifiable` |
| 2 | **Quote containment** — the quoted passage is in the cited source, byte-exact after canonicalisation | **fabricated quotes** | `unsupported` |
| 3 | **Entity grounding** — every number, version, date, acronym and proper noun in the claim is in the cited source | paraphrase drift | `unsupported` |
| 4 | **Polarity / value substitution** — the source isn't saying the opposite, or the same quantity with a different number | confident inversion | `contradicted` |
| 5 | **Prior leak** — the claim's facts appear in **no** fetched source | asserting from memory | `ungrounded` |

Canonicalisation handles what a raw substring test cannot: smart quotes, NBSP,
HTML entities, soft and line-break hyphenation, Unicode composition, and
punctuation as a separator — so `req/min`, `requests per minute` and
`requests-per-minute` all compare equal. The canonical form carries a
per-character byte map back to the original, so a match is reported as real byte
offsets into the text a human is reading. A receipt that highlights the wrong
passage is worse than no receipt.

**Every verdict carries a `next_action`.** A verdict is not an opinion, it is an
instruction: `re_retrieve` with a suggested query, `declare_unverifiable` with a
reason, `resolve_conflict` with a trust rule, or `drop`. Repair is a control loop,
not a retry.

### The compiler is the product's conscience

`compile_artifact` **structurally cannot** emit a claim whose verdict is not
`SUPPORTED`. Everything else lands in a named *"We could not verify"* section
with its reason. The headline metric is honest by construction — it can be zero.

---

![How a Verbatim run works](docs/diagrams/run.png)

The verifier is the one step with no language model in it. It is also the only
step that decides what may ship. `cfo.ai` sits outside the pipeline on purpose —
nothing in a run flows to it, and drawing an arrow would suggest otherwise.

## The control run, and why it is the real demo

`naive` mode performs the **same retrieval and the same verification**, but its
compiler ships every drafted claim regardless of verdict — which is what a
research agent does today. It has the information and ignores it.

The only difference between the two runs is **whether the compiler is allowed to
ship an unverified claim.** That is the whole experiment, and it is the honest
version of the A/B: same model, same sources, same budget, one changed decision.

A run on a real conflict:

> **How many requests per minute does the Anthropic free tier allow, and does the
> rate limit reset every minute?**
>
> Sources disagree: a third-party blog says **500**; Anthropic's own docs say
> **60**. Both quotes are verbatim, so the quote check passes on both. The
> conflict detector catches the disagreement, resolves it with a recorded rule —
> *the source whose host carries the entity the run is about wins, so
> `docs.anthropic.com` beats a blog about Anthropic* — drops the losing claim, and
> **prints the disagreement in the answer** rather than silently deciding it.

---

## Architecture

_See the diagram above. The pipeline is one run; the event log is the source of truth; the three partner tools observe from outside it._

**Backend: Rust** (Axum, Tokio, rusqlite, reqwest). Why: the verifier is the
product's core claim, and Rust is the right language for a component whose
correctness is the argument. The whole crate has no `unsafe`.

**Frontend: Next.js + TypeScript.** Why: it serves a reading surface, and a
reading surface is a web page.

### Durability

An **append-only event log is the only source of truth**; run state, the timeline
and the artifact are projections of it. Side effects settle-then-commit under
idempotency keys. A hard `kill -9` before an effect settles leaves no record of
it, so a resumed run redoes the work rather than guessing — and a redo is a no-op
at the tool boundary, so the effects ledger proves it repeated nothing.

This is the pattern that makes "state across steps, runs and failures" real rather
than claimed: **model-visible means logged, and user-visible means logged.**

---

## Hackathon relevance

**Track:** *Build an agent that works (literally)* — one track, every project
competes for the same prizes.

**Judging criteria and how this project answers them:**

| Criterion | Weight | How |
|---|---|---|
| The agent | 30% | plan → retrieve → claim → verify → repair → compile, end to end, with recovery driven by verdicts rather than retries |
| Use of neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai | 25% | each is structurally necessary, below |
| Demo video | 20% | one memorable beat: a claim that gets struck |
| Building in public | 15% | traced build sessions, dated build log, conflict the verifier caught |
| Usefulness & originality | 10% | audit mode checks *other* agents' answers |

### The three partners, each with a real role

**neatlogs** — one nested JSON trace per run posted to `POST /v1/trace`
(documentation explicitly supports Rust via this path; there is no Rust SDK).
Span kinds are chosen so the dashboard tells the product's story without
narration: `WORKFLOW` root → `AGENT` (planner, repairer) → `RETRIEVER` (query +
documents) → `TOOL` (fetch) → `LLM` (model + tokens) → and, crucially,
**`GUARDRAIL` for every verification check with `passed` and `score`**. A failed
verification is natively an error span in neatlogs, so the argument of the product
is visible in someone else's tool. Naive and verified runs share a
`neatlogs.session.id` and are diffed side by side.

**Entire** — enabled from the first commit. The agent commits its artifacts
(`answer.md`, `claims.json`), so **`entire why answer.md:34`** reveals the session
behind any sentence: provenance of code, meeting provenance of claims.

**cfo.ai** — unit economics for the agent, built in cfo.ai itself and readable
by anyone: **https://cfo.ai/s/mAotSQsQFqUlV-xU**

That sheet is where the numbers in this README come from, and it labels its own
inputs rather than presenting them as facts: model cost per report is *measured*
at $0.007, Enterprise price and usage are *estimates*, and cash and opex are
*planning assumptions*. Its output: blended ARPU $239.10, gross margin **83.4%**,
break-even at **301 paying customers**, and runway of 49.4 months in the Base
scenario against 13.7 in Downside.

One caveat it also states: the Enterprise price is a guess and, at a 10% mix, it
drives most of the blended ARPU. Unit economics are not this business's risk.
Distribution is.

eatlogs write key

### Install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/PhiBao/verbatim
cd verbatim
cargo build --release --workspace
cd web && pnpm install && cd ..
```

### Configure

Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and fill it in. `.env` is gitignored and never
committed.

| Variable | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LITELLM_BASE_URL` / `LITELLM_API_KEY` / `LITELLM_MODEL` | one model | the hackathon gateway, or Bedrock |
| `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` | for traces | project key from app.neatlogs.com |
| `NEATLOGS_PROJECT` | for traces | project **name** — a write key identifies a user, not a project |
| `VERBATIM_RETRIEVAL` | default `corpus` | `corpus` = pinned snapshot; `live` = real web retrieval |

### Commands

```bash
# The API and the reading surface
cargo run --release --bin engine          # http://127.0.0.1:8787
cd web && pnpm dev                        # http://localhost:3000, proxies /api to the engine

# Check one claim against one source — no model involved
verbatim verify \
  --claim "The Anthropic Messages API rate limits are measured in requests per minute, input tokens per minute, and output tokens per minute." \
  --quote "The rate limits for the Messages API are measured in requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (ITPM), and output tokens per minute (OTPM) for each model class." \
  --source https://docs.anthropic.com/en/api/rate-limits

# Audit an answer that came from somewhere else
verbatim audit --answer "..." --source https://example.test/a

# See the plan without spending anything
verbatim run "what are the Anthropic rate limits?" --dry-run
```

### Test

```bash
cargo test --workspace      # 39 tests
cargo clippy --workspace    # warnings only
```

The verifier's tests are the ones that matter, because they are the ones that
would let a stranger catch us lying. They include the cases a naive
implementation gets wrong: a quote with one number changed, a quote with smart
quotes, a soft hyphenation, a dead source, and a claim whose facts appear in no
fetched source.

---

## Demo

| | |
|---|---|
| **Live app** | https://verbatim-neathack.fly.dev |
| **Demo video** | [youtu.be/Zifq7diJUUg](https://youtu.be/Zifq7diJUUg) — 2m42s |
| **Business model** | https://cfo.ai/s/mAotSQsQFqUlV-xU — the real cfo.ai sheet |
| **Entire checkpoint** | [938a4a461991](https://entire.io/gh/PhiBao/verbatim/commit/938a4a461991046258f57523d69f67d624d3f76b) — `01M4KQNDHEF4YFPRHX4E13YQ8W` |
| **Run with receipts** | [/ \?run=02078eb3-48a3-4aa5-94ab-6a01f9edfc22](https://verbatim-neathack.fly.dev/?run=02078eb3-48a3-4aa5-94ab-6a01f9edfc22) |

A real run against the live web, unaided:

| | |
|---|---|
| claims checked | **57** |
| verified | **47** |
| contradicted | **2** |
| unsupported | **8** |
| sources read | **39** |
| runs | verified and control, same question |
| traces ingested | **29**, zero rejected |
| side effects | **39**, zero duplicated on resume |

The 10 rejected claims are the product working. Eight were paraphrased rather
than quoted; two stated a different value than the source. A human reading the
same 39 pages would almost certainly have shipped at least one of them.

1. **Ask** a question where sources disagree.
2. **Watch** the timeline: plan → searches → fetches → claims → verdicts.
3. **The beat:** a confident claim flips to `CONTRADICTED` and strikes through.
4. **The receipts page:** click any sentence → the quote, the byte offsets, the
   SHA-256 of the source, and the score.
5. **Audit mode:** paste someone else's answer with its sources and get the same
   ledger. Verbatim does not compete with deep-research tools; it checks them.

### Reproducibility

The demo runs against a **pinned corpus** — a snapshot of real pages fetched
during the hackathon by `engine snapshot`, stored with their SHA-256. A recorded
run replays byte-for-byte and cannot break because a website changed. `live` mode
is what production uses. Both are labelled in the UI and stated here.

---

## Verification — what is real, what is not

**Real, live, and externally verifiable:**
- The verifier. Five deterministic checks, no model. `verbatim verify` runs the
  same code path the agent runs, so anyone can reproduce any verdict from a
  terminal.
- Traces. 29 real traces ingested from the deployed process, including
  `GUARDRAIL` spans for every failed check. Visible in the public neatlogs
  project.
- The 57-claim run above, reproducible against live Tavily retrieval.
- The control run. Same retrieval, same model, same budget; only the compile rule
  differs.
- Cost accounting. Measured per run against the gateway's own usage.
- Conflict detection and resolution, with the deciding rule recorded.

**Deterministic by design, and labelled as such:**
- The pinned corpus. Real fetches, snapshotted during the hackathon.

**Not built, and not claimed:**
- Live retrieval depends on Tavily and the LiteLLM gateway. When live search
  returns nothing usable, the run falls back to the pinned corpus and says so in
  the trace, rather than failing or silently shrinking.
- Audit mode checks **grounding**, not **support**: an arbitrary answer carries no
  quotes, so the strongest deterministic check available is whether each
  sentence's facts appear in a source we read. We do not claim to verify support
  without a quote to check.
- No multi-agent crew. A single agent plus an independent verifier is the thesis;
  multi-agent has documented failure modes and would dilute it.

---

## Security

- **SSRF.** The agent chooses its own URLs, so every fetch is untrusted. Requests
  are confined to public `http(s)` on ports 80/443: private, loopback, link-local,
  multicast, unspecified and **bracketed IPv6 literals** are rejected, every
  redirect hop is re-validated, the body is capped at 2 MB, and script/style/svg
  content is stripped before matching.
- **Prompt injection.** Fetched content is untrusted and reaches the model. It is
  never treated as instructions, and a claim is only as good as the deterministic
  quote check against the raw bytes — so injected text that tries to look like
  evidence is measured against the source it claims to come from.
- **Secrets.** `.env` is gitignored. The neatlogs key is ingest-only (it can POST
  traces, never read them back). No secret ever reaches the repo, and trace
  bodies are written to `/tmp` on rejection, never to a log that ships.
- **Budget.** The model gateway enforces a $20 shared ceiling; the agent also
  enforces its own 2-cent-per-run ceiling so one runaway loop cannot spend the
  team's allowance.
- **Failure states.** A dead source is `unverifiable`, not silently absent. A
  budget breach stops the run and returns a *partial verified* answer with an
  explicit banner. Malformed model output is rejected, not guessed at.

---

## Limitations and what's next

- The naive control run is honest but narrow: it proves the compiler's gate
  matters, not that the retrieval is good.
- Authority resolution is one stateable rule. A richer model would weigh
  recency, corroboration count and primary-vs-secondary explicitly.
- Two-witness corroboration (two blind claimers, one adjudicator) is designed and
  not built.

---

## Build log

`hackathon.md` is the running, dated log with every failure and fix, including
the ones the tests missed: an SSRF hole that accepted bracketed IPv6 literals,
`<style>` content leaking into matching text, a `blocking_lock` panic inside a
tokio handler, and the 8 KB ingest ceiling that was found by bisecting a live
payload.
# hackathon.md — neatHack build log

> Running evidence log for **Verbatim**. Maintained per the neatHack build-log
> skill: dated entries, planned vs completed work, tests that actually ran, and
> failures that remain. No secrets, no private traces.

- **Project:** Verbatim — a research agent where every sentence carries a receipt.
  If we didn't fetch it, we didn't say it.
- **Problem:** agents self-certify their own success. 3–13% of deep-research
  citation URLs never existed (arXiv 2604.03173); best factual F1 under clean-room
  eval is 0.337 (arXiv 2606.11337).
- **Team:** solo — PhiBao (kiter2509@gmail.com)
- **Event:** neatHack, Oct 10–12 2026, one track ("an agent that works, literally").
  Submission: Oct 12, 19:00–23:55 IST, quote-tweet of the official neatlogs post.
- **Stack:** Rust (Axum, rusqlite, Bedrock Converse) · Next.js + TypeScript ·
  neatlogs HTTP trace injection · Entire checkpoints · cfo.ai business model.

## Sponsor usage

| Tool | Role in the project | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **neatlogs** | One nested trace per run. Every verification check is a `GUARDRAIL` span with `passed`/`score`, so a failed verification is an error span in the dashboard. Naive and verified runs of the same question are diffed side by side. | trace ids recorded per run; dashboard project `neathack` |
| **Entire** | Enabled from the first commit. The agent commits `answer.md` + `claims.json`, so `entire why answer.md:34` reveals the session behind any sentence. | checkpoint link + ID, recorded below |
| **cfo.ai** | Unit economics for the agent: price per verified report, inference cost per report, gross margin, Base/Growth scenarios, runway. | shared scenario link + screenshots |

## Build log

### 2026-10-10

**14:20 IST — foundation (completed)**
- Rust workspace created: `crates/engine` (Axum service + agent core) and
  `crates/cli` (`verbatim`, the agent-facing CLI).
- Dependency spike on `aws-sdk-bedrockruntime` resolved; the LLM sits behind an
  `Llm` trait so a provider swap is a one-file change.

**Verifier v1 (completed, 26 tests passing)**
`cargo test -p engine --lib` → 26 passed, 0 failed.

- `text.rs` — canonical text form with a per-character byte map back to the
  original, so receipts highlight the real passage. Handles smart quotes, NBSP,
  HTML entities, soft-hyphenation, line-break hyphenation, combining marks and
  punctuation-as-separator (`req/min` ≡ `req per minute`).
- `verify.rs` — five deterministic checks, **no LLM in any of them**:
  1. source available
  2. quote containment (byte-exact after canonicalisation)
  3. entity grounding against the cited source
  4. polarity / value substitution
  5. prior leak — the claim's facts appear in *no* fetched source
- Verdicts: `supported`, `contradicted`, `unsupported`, `conflict`,
  `ungrounded`, `unverifiable`. Every verdict carries a `next_action`, so the
  repairer is a control loop rather than a retry.

**Known failures and how they were fixed (recorded honestly)**
- First cut put the prior-leak check *before* quote containment, so a claim whose
  number appeared nowhere was reported as `ungrounded` even when the source was
  clearly talking about the same quantity. Reordered: containment first, then
  diagnose *why* it failed.
- Offsets were reported as `raw.len()` when a match ran to the end of the source,
  which highlighted trailing punctuation. Fixed by mapping per-character byte
  ranges instead of a single index map.

# PreJudge: get roasted before the judges do

**Live: https://3-82-224-157.sslip.io** · neatHack (Oct 10–12, 2026) · team QBITS

PreJudge is an AI agent that audits a hackathon submission before the real judges see it. Paste a
public GitHub repo URL and in about 5 seconds you get a judge-readiness score (0–100) mapped to the
official neatHack rubric, a fix list ordered by the points each fix is worth, and a short roast
that has to quote facts from your repo. Ask for the deep check and the agent downloads a read-only
copy of the repo, pulls the claims out of your README and tries to prove or disprove each one with
`file:line` evidence, then rescores. It never runs the audited code, and the README is never
accepted as proof of its own claims. The result is a shareable page with a roast card (PNG + link
preview).

> 🎬 **Demo video (≤ 3 min):** _link coming Monday, Oct 12_

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[Repo URL] --> Q
    subgraph Q[Quick phase · about 5 s · at most 1 LLM call]
        G[GitHub API: repo, README, tree, commits, Entire refs] --> C[13 deterministic rubric checks]
        L[Link checker: SSRF-safe] --> C
        V[Video length from metadata] --> C
        C --> S1[Deterministic score] --> R1[Verdict + roast, fact-checked]
    end
    R1 --> P1[(SQLite: quick_ready)]
    P1 -->|Run deep check| D
    subgraph D[Deep phase · queued one at a time]
        T[Tarball, read-only, 30 MB cap] --> X[Extract README claims]
        X --> PS[Code pre-searches every claim]
        PS --> A[Agent tools: search_repo, read_file, list_files, get_commits, check_link]
        A --> J[Each claim: verified / unverified / contradicted + evidence]
        J --> S2[Rescore + capped estimates] --> R2[Final verdict]
    end
    R2 --> P2[(SQLite: complete)]
    P2 --> O[Result page, roast card PNG, /r/id link preview]
```

**Quick phase** (`backend/app/audit.py`): reads the repo through the GitHub API and runs 13
deterministic checks from `backend/app/tools/rubric.py`. They cover commits inside the hackathon
window, neatlogs in the dependencies, trace links, Entire checkpoints, the cfo.ai plan, demo video
length, building-in-public posts, before/after numbers, a failure-and-recovery run, dead links and
prompt injection. Then one LLM call writes the verdict and roast. The result is saved straight
away, so the deep phase never holds it up.

**Deep phase** (`backend/app/agent/loop.py`): downloads the repo tarball once (size-capped;
binaries, `node_modules`, vendored code, lockfiles, symlinks and path traversal are skipped),
extracts the README's claims and verifies each one with the agent tools in
`backend/app/agent/tools.py`. `search_repo` (`backend/app/tools/search.py`) returns `file:line`
snippets with context. A claim only counts as verified when the agent cites evidence it actually
saw in the code; citing the README is not enough.

**Scoring** (`backend/app/scoring.py`) is plain code with the rubric weights: agent 30%, neatlogs +
Entire + cfo.ai 25%, demo video 20%, building in public 15%, usefulness 10%. The LLM never sets the
score. The two things code can't measure (agent quality, usefulness) get an LLM estimate that must
cite evidence. It is labelled "estimated" and capped at 80% of those points. When a check can't be
verified automatically (for example, no Entire checkpoints found), it isn't scored and its weight
moves to the rest of the category. That way PreJudge never takes points away for something it
couldn't see.

**Safety:** repo content is untrusted data in delimited blocks. Instructions hidden in a README
are detected, flagged on the result page and cannot move the score. Links are fetched behind an
SSRF guard: `_host_problem()` in `backend/app/tools/links.py` refuses any host that resolves to a
private, loopback, link-local (this includes the cloud metadata address 169.254.169.254),
reserved, multicast or unspecified address. Redirects are followed by hand, so every hop is
checked again.

**Running on the Groq free tier** (`backend/app/llm.py`): it rotates across models and schedules
calls from the rate-limit headers. On a failure, `_classify()` sorts the error (for example
`rate_limited` for a 429), and `_on_failure()` puts that model on a cooldown for as long as the
`retry-after` header says (read by `_retry_after()`). The call then moves to the next model,
recorded as an `llm.<purpose>.fallback` step. Other errors get exponential backoff with jitter. Deep checks wait for budget rather than drop to a weaker model. Failures are
recorded as steps, and the user always gets at least a partial report. Per-IP limits, a deep-queue
cap and a per-repo cooldown protect the shared budget (`backend/app/limits.py`).

## How we use neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai

### neatlogs
Every audit is traced with the [neatlogs](https://neatlogs.com) SDK (`backend/app/tracing.py`):
each LLM call, tool call, retry, fallback and failure is recorded under the audit id as the session
id. Traces are tagged `real`/`test` and `prod`/`dev`, and secrets are masked before anything leaves
the process. The before/after numbers below come from these traces, and the M2 baseline's 16 failed LLM
calls showed up there too.

### Entire
> ⏳ **To fill in once Entire is enabled in this repo:** checkpoint link
> entire.io/gh/DurgaPritam/neatHack-QBITS-/commit/FULL_SHA and the checkpoint ID.

We set this repo up following the [neatHack Entire guide](https://hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026/).
PreJudge also checks Entire for other teams: it reads the `Entire-Checkpoint` commit trailers and
the pushed `refs/entire/checkpoints` storage described in the
[Entire docs](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/checkpoint-storage).

### cfo.ai
We built the business plan in cfo.ai: [shared model](https://cfo.ai/s/xBCsLLiMtconXUBf) ·
summary in [docs/business-plan.md](docs/business-plan.md).

- **Pricing:** monthly licenses at $199 / $499 / $999, pay-per-event audits at $49 / $149, and a
  free tier for individual teams.
- **Costs:** AI costs $0.0095 per audit, blended (measured in our traces: $0.005 quick, $0.02
  deep), and hosting is $20/month.
- **Revenue:** paid sales start Jan 2027. In the Main scenario that reaches $24,651/month by Sep
  2028 at a 97% gross margin.
- **Runway:** bootstrapped. The Main scenario is profitable every month from Feb 2027 and never
  runs out of cash (its lowest point is $1,748).

The model changed our decisions. Replacing a $0.40-per-audit AI guess with the measured cost moved
break-even 9 months earlier (v2 → v3).

## Evidence

All numbers come from real runs. Audit ids double as neatlogs session ids. The full log is in
[EVIDENCE.md](EVIDENCE.md).

### Before → after

Before → after on openai/swarm: first result in 52s before the two-speed redesign, 5.5s after it.

| Change (repo) | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| M2 model + loop changes (openai/swarm) | 40,086 tokens, 106 s, 0 of 8 claims checked, 16 failed LLM calls | 19,066 tokens, 52 s, claims verified with `file:line` evidence |
| Two-speed audits: time to first result (openai/swarm) | 52 s | 5.5 s (quick phase, 4,094 tokens) |
| Tarball + `search_repo` + code pre-search: verified claims (huggingface/smolagents) | 1 of 8 | 6 of 8 (`b8e64c021d56`) |
| Quick phase capped at one LLM call (openai/swarm) | 4,094 tokens | 2,154 tokens, 5.5 s |
| Production, this repo (`29def6e19f64`) | — | quick 2,173 tokens / 5.3 s; deep 17,232 tokens / 40.5 s; 6 of 6 claims verified |

### Failure and recovery in production (audit `29def6e19f64`)

During the deep check of this repo, the claim-judging call `llm.verify` on `qwen/qwen3.8-27b`
**failed with a Groq 429 (rate limit)**. The agent backed off, retried on the fallback model
`openai/gpt-oss-120b` (3 calls, 9,018 prompt tokens) and finished the audit: 46/100 with 6 of 6
claims verified. The failed call is a recorded step on the public result page
https://3-82-224-157.sslip.io/a/29def6e19f64 and in the neatlogs trace for session `29def6e19f6(eval):1: ==== not found

# PreJudge: business plan (final model, v3)

PreJudge is an AI agent that audits hackathon projects against the judging rubric before the real
judges do: a score, a fix list, README claims checked against the code, and a roast. This plan
covers **Oct 2026 – Sep 2028 (24 months), in USD**. Free pilots run in Q4 2026; paid sales start in
**Jan 2027**.

Built with cfo.ai: [shared model](https://cfo.ai/s/xBCsLLiMtconXUBf) · raw notes:
[cfo-ai-notes-raw.md](cfo-ai-notes-raw.md)

> **Assumption to confirm:** starting cash is a **$2,000 placeholder**. The plan holds as long as
> we start with at least about $250 (lowest cash in Main is $1,748).

## Customers and pricing

| Plan | Price | Audits included | Monthly churn | New customers, first paid month (growth/mo) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hackathon organizers | $199/mo | 150/mo | 6% | 1 (8%) |
| Accelerators & incubators | $499/mo | 40/mo | 3% | 0.5 (6%) |
| Companies (internal hackathons) | $999/mo | 80/mo | 2.5% | 0.25 (6%) |
| Pay per event | $49 up to 50 teams · $149 for 51–300 teams | one per team | — | 4 events in Jan 2027 (+8%/mo) |
| Free tier (individual teams) | $0 | 5,000/mo in total | — | growth channel, booked as marketing |

Event mix assumption: 60% small (about 25 teams), 40% large (about 120 teams). That gives an
average of $89 and about 63 audits per event.

## Costs

| Cost | v3 assumption |
|---|---|
| AI per audit | **$0.005 quick, $0.02 deep, 70% quick-only = $0.0095 blended** |
| Hosting | $20/mo minimum + $2 per 1,000 audits (estimate); about $25/mo by Sep 2028 |
| Card fees | 3% of revenue (about 10× the AI bill) |
| Marketing | $1,000/mo from launch |
| Free tier AI | about $48/mo (5,000 audits × $0.0095) |
| Team | Founder unpaid. Hires in Jun 2027 ($3,000/mo), Oct 2027 ($2,500), Mar 2028 ($3,000), each +15% overhead |

**Where the AI cost comes from.** Our neatlogs traces measured about 2.6k LLM tokens per quick audit
and about 15k per deep audit (see [EVIDENCE.md](../EVIDENCE.md)). At Groq's list price for our

# release-gate-agent **An autonomous Android release agent that tests what actually shipped.** Give it the currently-shipped `old.apk` and the release-candidate `new.apk`. It diffs the *compiled* binaries, decides which user journeys that change puts at risk, drives a real Android emulator through those journeys on both builds, writes an evidence-backed report with a code-level fix, and then **stops at a human release gate**: the release does not ship until a person clicks Allow. Built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) (Oct 10–12, 2026). #neatHack · **[▶ Demo video](https://youtu.be/AEPnlF2-uyQ)** · **[Submission summary](SUBMISSION.md)** ## Why Release testing today either crawls the UI blindly (Robo-style crawlers), or reads the source/PR diff to decide what to test. Neither one looks at what actually ships. Compiled output can drift from source (build flags, R8/ProGuard, multi-module merges), and source-diff tools don't work at all for the people who most often sign off a build: QA and release engineers who were handed an APK. Diffing the compiled build doesn't have either problem. The bugs that matter most are the quiet ones. Both demo scenarios are real-world classes of regression that **don't crash and don't throw**: a SharedPreferences rename without a migration silently logs every existing user out (scenario 1) or deletes their saved notes (scenario 2) the moment they update. Fresh installs work fine, so a typical "install and smoke test" pass misses both of them. ## What the agent does, end to end ```mermaid flowchart LR A["diff_apks
manifest + per-dex string pool
+ per-class hashes"] --> B["Plan
which journeys does
this change put at risk?"] B --> C["Execute on emulator
install / launch / tap /
observe, on both builds"] C -->|tool error| R["Recover
wait for device,
retry once, re-observe"] R --> C C --> D["Verify
compare end states
old vs new, with evidence"] D --> E["write_report
results table, root cause,
suggested fix (code)"] E --> F{"request_release_approval
PASS / REGRESSION_DETECTED /
INCONCLUSIVE"} F -- "human: Allow" --> G(["ships"]) F -- "human: Deny" --> H(["blocked"]) ``` - **Planning:** chooses a small set of journeys from the diff: always the in-place upgrade journey, usually a fresh-install control to tell an upgrade-only bug from a bug that hits everyone, plus whatever the diff calls for. - **Tool use:** 13 MCP tools over adb and aapt (`tools/server.mjs`). - **State:** the device itself is the state. It sets up app state on the old build, upgrades in place, and checks whether that state survived. - **Recovery:** adb failures come back to the agent as tool errors. The prompt requires wait-for-device, one retry, and recording each failure in the report. - **Verification:** a verdict needs device evidence (screenshot, screen state, logcat). With none, the only allowed verdict is `INCONCLUSIVE`. - **Human gate:** `request_release_approval` is enforced by the harness (Claude Agent SDK `canUseTool`), not by the agent promising to stop. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR You(["Release engineer"]) -->|"drop 2 APKs, Allow/Deny"| UI["control-panel
(web UI, SSE)"] UI -->|spawn| AG["agent/run.mjs
Claude Agent SDK"] AG -->|"events"| UI AG <-->|"MCP over HTTP"| T["tools/server.mjs
diff_apks, adb_*, write_report,
request_release_approval"] T <-->|adb| EMU["Android emulator"] AG -. "every turn, tool call,
tokens, cost" .-> NL[("neatlogs")] ``` ## How we used the sponsor tools ### neatlogs: trace every run, then use the traces to improve the agent `agent/run.mjs` wraps the Claude Agent SDK with `wrapClaudeAgentSDK`. Every run is one neatlogs trace containing each model turn (input, output, tokens) and each MCP tool call, tagged by `prompt:`, `toolset:` and `scenario:` so versions can be filtered and compared side by side. **Before → after.** We read the v1 trace of the first real run and found three problems: 1. `adb_launch` returned before the activity was up, so the next screen dump saw `mCurrentFocus=null` and the agent had to dump again (launch → dump → dump, 4 times in one run). 2. Every launch and tap was followed by a separate dump call. The tool outputs were small, so the cost came from the number of turns: each turn re-reads the whole context. 3. There was no "couldn't test" verdict. A smoke run with no device reported `REGRESSION_DETECTED` from the diff alone. v2 (`prompts/v2-evidence-first.md` plus the v2 toolset) fixed all three: launch waits for the resumed activity, launch and tap return the resulting screen, the screen state is compact with tap centres, `INCONCLUSIVE` was added, and the prompt was tightened and given explicit recovery rules. The v1 toolset is still selectable (`--prompt v1-baseline`), so the baseline can be re-run as-is. **Result (8 real emulator runs, both scenarios, 2 runs per version per scenario):** | | v1 baseline | v2 evidence-first | change | |---|---|---|---| | Correct verdict | 4/4 | 4/4 | same | | Turns per run | 39.0 | 24.2 | **-38%** | | Wall time per run | 99.4 s | 81.7 s | **-18%** | | Cost per run* | $0.264 | $0.205 | **-22%** | | Cached input tokens per run | 214,224 | 138,738 | **-35%** | | Output tokens per run | 6,042 | 4,844 | -20% |
Per-scenario breakdown | Prompt | Scenario | Runs | Verdicts | Turns (avg) | Tool calls (avg) | Time s (avg) | Cost $ (avg) | Cached input tokens (avg) | Output tokens (avg) | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | v1-baseline | auth-logout | 2 | REGRESSION_DETECTED×2 | 40.0 | 39.0 | 101.8 | 0.262 | 223297 | 6058 | | v1-baseline | notes-data-loss | 2 | REGRESSION_DETECTED×2 | 38.0 | 37.0 | 97.1 | 0.267 | 205151 | 6027 | | v2-evidence-first | auth-logout | 2 | REGRESSION_DETECTED×2 | 24.0 | 23.0 | 77.5 | 0.198 | 117535 | 4660 | | v2-evidence-first | notes-data-loss | 2 | REGRESSION_DETECTED×2 | 24.5 | 23.5 | 85.8 | 0.213 | 159941 | 5028 |
\* Cost is the `total_cost_usd` the Claude Agent SDK reports per run (standard API pricing for the tokens used), also visible on each neatlogs trace. Filter traces in neatlogs by the `prompt:v1-baseline` / `prompt:v2-evidence-first` tags to see the two sides. Reproduce: `scripts/bench.sh auth-logout:v1-baseline auth-logout:v2-evidence-first`. ### Entire: inside the agent, and in how we built it - **entire-graph inside the agent.** `diff_apks` says *which compiled class changed*. When the app's source is available (`--source`), the agent's `source_impact` tool runs `entire graph impact` on that class to find which screens depend on it (`AuthManager` → Splash/Login/Dashboard). The agent then picks journeys from that, as in the [failure-recovery run](evidence/failure-recovery). - **Checkpoints for the coding agent.** Entire is enabled for Claude Code in this repo. Checkpoint [`01M4JN7HHKQ28WF2HYV3VGEN0T`](https://entire.io/gh/Shivam-sopho/release-gate-agent/commit/d94f4ef370004e38a3259b8deb2840d7201a119f) captures the session that fixed the control panel's INCONCLUSIVE verdict display: prompt, decisions and diff. - **Trails.** Runners tailored to this repo review every Trail. With `--trail ` the release agent posts its verdict, evidence summary, cost and gate decision to that Trail, so code review and on-device release evidence sit on one page with a human # Roster

> Roster is an agent that runs performance reviews for your AI coding agents.

It reads every session your coding agents recorded with [Entire](https://entire.io), and for each one works out:
- what it cost
- whether its change survived
- whether it was reverted, or reworked by a person

Then it tests a better setup on your own past tasks, and ships that setup only if nothing regresses.

**Live:**
- [roster-five-chi.vercel.app](https://roster-five-chi.vercel.app)
- [our own AI team's review](https://roster-five-chi.vercel.app/r/rajkaria/roster)
- [all reviews](https://roster-five-chi.vercel.app/r)

## What it does

A **setup** is a coding-agent harness, a model and a rules file, for example Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5 and your `CLAUDE.md`. Roster:

1. **Reviews:** it scores every recorded session of every setup.
   - It prices the session from its tokens.
   - It checks whether its lines survived at `HEAD`, were reverted, or were reworked by a person.
   - It checks whether the session ran unattended.
   - Setups are compared on tasks of similar difficulty (Mantel–Haenszel across difficulty terciles). This is **evidence level A, observational**: it can name a suspect but proves nothing on its own.
2. **Replays:** it reruns a setup's real past tasks at their parent commit, in a sandbox with no future history.
   - Each task runs under the incumbent setup and under candidate setups.
   - Each attempt is graded with the tests the team kept, the full suite, a scope guard and a blind diff judge.
   - **Level B.**
3. **Gates:** a deterministic gate promotes a candidate only if nothing regresses. The model decides what to try next, and the gate decides what ships.
4. **Tests forward:** new tasks, written and hashed before the decision, run through the old and the new setup side by side and are graded blind. **Level C.**
5. **Books:** it writes the AI team's spend per setup into the company's [cfo.ai](https://cfo.ai) plan, with a hire-or-scale scenario. *(Pending: needs the cfo.ai connection.)*

Every Roster run is traced in [neatlogs](https://neatlogs.com).

## This repo is the experiment

Four coding-agent setups built this repo, assigned to tasks by a seeded shuffle and recorded by Entire ([`setups/`](setups)):

| Setup | Harness | Model | Rules |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Claude Code | Opus 5.5 | default |
| B | Claude Code | Sonnet 5.5 | default |
| C | Claude Code | Haiku 5.5 | default |
| D | Claude Code | Sonnet 5.5 | default + strict |

The candidates run Claude Code on DeepSeek:

| Candidate | Model |
|---|---|
| E | DeepSeek Flash |
| F | DeepSeek V4 Pro |

The test was fixed in advance in [`experiments/PREREGISTRATION.md`](experiments/PREREGISTRATION.md):
- The 40 forward tasks and their acceptance tests were frozen before the first review. The hashes are in [`experiments/FREEZE.txt`](experiments/FREEZE.txt).
- Every change since then is a dated amendment, including two protocol deviations and the first review's weak evidence.

**Status, from [`docs/FACTS.md`](docs/FACTS.md):**
- **Level A:** Roster reviewed its own repo (61 sessions, 4 setups) and found **no suspect** (odds ratio 4.23, p = 1.000).
- **Level B:** Review 1 promoted **E** over B. The two tied at zero hidden-test passes, and E was cheaper. That is weak evidence, and amendment 7 says so: even the incumbent failed its own replayed tasks. The replay bug behind it is being fixed.
- **Level C:** the forward run of B against E is in progress. Results will be published whatever they show.

## Roster caught its own silent mistakes

Reviewing its own build, Roster's v1 output was green but wrong six times. Each was fixed by a recorded agent task:
- It saw 3 setups where there were 4.
- It priced Haiku sessions at $0.
- It dropped the hidden tests of 16 of 23 tasks.
- It counted one prompt as three.
- Its replays failed without a reason.
- It priced DeepSeek runs at Claude rates.

The build log in [`hackathon.md`](hackathon.md) has the details.

## Run it

```bash
bun install
bun src/cli.ts review https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> --observational   # level A, read-only, no model calls
bun src/cli.ts run <repo> --budget 5                                        # coordinator: plan, replay, gate (DeepSeek)
bun src/cli.ts forward --backlog <file> --pair OLD,NEW                      # paired forward run, blind grading
```

**Requirements:**
- The repo must record sessions with Entire (`entire/checkpoints/v1` or `refs/entire/checkpoints/*`).
- Replays need the Claude Code CLI.
- Roster's own reasoning uses DeepSeek: set `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` in `.env`.

[`docs/DESIGN.md`](docs/DESIGN.md) is the engineering contract.

## Built with

| Tool | What it does in Roster |
|---|---|
| **Entire** | The data Roster reads (sessions, prompts, tokens, model, commit), and the recorder for every session that built Roster |
| **neatlogs** | Traces every Roster run, from ingest to each replay attempt and gate decision |
| **cfo.ai** | Where Roster books the AI team as a department of the company plan *(connection pending)* |

## Limits

- Tests are a proxy for value.
- Level A on a young repo is mostly "insufficient data" or "no suspect", by design.
- Replays of public repos must run in isolated VMs; local replays are only for repos you trust.

MIT

# Crashtest

**Find the bugs your users would hit, before they hit them.**

Most bugs that reach users are not in code nobody tested. They are in paths nobody walked: rejecting instead of approving, the empty account, the second tab, someone else's id in the URL. Crashtest is a macOS app with an autonomous agent that walks those paths for you.

Give it a GitHub repo and it:

1. **Maps the app from its code** — screens, actions, API operations, background jobs, integrations, roles, entity lifecycles, limits.
2. **Writes every scenario a user can do or live through**, ranked P1–P3 and grouped by user journey.
3. **Runs them for real** — clones the app, boots it on your Mac or on your own server (VDS), drives it in a browser, and reports what broke with a screenshot, the root cause at `file:line`, and a suggested diff. It never edits your code.

Built during [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) (Oct 10–12, 2026). Build log: [hackathon.md](hackathon.md).

> 🔴 **Live now:** [watch Crashtest test neatroots](http://34.238.91.131:8080) — every dot is one scenario; the yellow spark is the one being tried right now.

## neatlogs asked us to test their own product

After our first post, neatlogs' head of product engineering [replied](https://x.com/kurokotetsuyami/status/2108943094809071674): *"run this on neatroots, & share your findings with me"*. So we did. Crashtest mapped [neatlogs/neatroots](https://github.com/neatlogs/neatroots) into **581 scenarios across 12 user journeys** in under 5 minutes, booted it on a 2 GB server by itself, and ran **every one of them: ✅ 316 · ❌ 158 · ⏭ 107**. We checked the broken verdicts by hand against the source: **21 real bugs**, among them turning steering off still letting a halt note stop the agent, one bad regex in a check freezing the whole server for 33 seconds, `retention.days: 0` in `config.yaml` deleting every run on start, and a large import upload crashing the server. Each one has repro steps, `file:line` and a fix: [docs/evidence/findings-neatroots.md](docs/evidence/findings-neatroots.md).

![Crashtest × neatroots](docs/evidence/neatroots-findings.png)

## What it found on its first real target

On [TonyMckes/conduit-realworld-example-app](https://github.com/TonyMckes/conduit-realworld-example-app), a well-known RealWorld implementation, Crashtest mapped 39 surfaces into **294 scenarios** across 9 journeys in 143 s, booted the app from scratch (local Postgres, generated `.env`, API + frontend) and ran **every one of them**:

**✅ 180 passed · ❌ 104 broken · ⏭ 10 skipped** — and the 104 broken scenarios trace back to **34 files**. Among them:

- **Saving your settings with a blank password replaces your password.** `backend/controllers/user.js:36` checks `password !== undefined || password !== ""`, which is always true.
- **Any bad, forged or expired token crashes the request with a 500** instead of a 401 — 14 scenarios, one error path in `backend/middleware/authentication.js`.
- **Tokens never expire and survive logout and password changes** (`backend/helper/jwt.js`).
- **A comment can be deleted through any article's URL** — `backend/controllers/comments.js` ignores the slug. Found on the first run and found again, independently, in the full run.
- **Duplicate usernames, self-follows, double-click double-publishes**, negative `limit`/`offset` → 500 with raw DB errors.

We checked the top findings against the source by hand. Details, diffs and screenshots: [docs/evidence/findings-conduit.md](docs/evidence/findings-conduit.md).

It is not tied to one app: on [thedevs-network/kutt](https://github.com/thedevs-network/kutt) (URL shortener) the same build mapped 50 surfaces into **359 scenarios across 11 journeys** in 144 s, then ran all 141 P1 scenarios: **✅ 97 · ❌ 31 · ⏭ 13**. Worst one: deleting a domain "without its links" deletes every link on it, because the checkbox sanitizer passes the string `"false"` through as truthy. [docs/evidence/findings-kutt.md](docs/evidence/findings-kutt.md).

## How it works

```
GitHub link ─► Intake ─► Inventory agent ─► Scenario writer ─► [Start] ─► Local │ VDS
               clone,     Sonnet 5.5,        Haiku 5.5,                     │
               products   read-only tools    parallel per journey           ▼
                                                              Bootstrap agent ─► Sweep agent
                                                              boots the app      one scenario at a time,
                                                              (shell, logs,      Playwright browser + API,
                                                              ports, recovery)   verdict + root cause + diff
```

- **Agents** run on the [Claude Agent SDK](https://docs.claude.com/en/api/agent-sdk/overview) with a per-phase tool set: the inventory agent can only read; the bootstrap and sweep agents operate the app through Crashtest's own MCP tools (`shell`, `start_background`, `read_log`, `expose_port`, `http_get`).
- **Local and VDS are the same to the agent.** Both runtimes implement those tools; the VDS runtime works over SSH and tunnels the app's ports back so the browser on your Mac can drive it.
- **Recovery.** If the app stops answering mid-run, Crashtest restarts it with the commands the bootstrap agent used and carries on. Services run in the foreground and are always stopped at the end, even if you quit mid-run.
- **Chat.** Ask about the app, hand over `.env` values or server details (stored encrypted in the macOS Keychain), or start a run from the conversation.

# Migration Parachute

A schema migration can be correct and still take down a service. Migration Parachute is an agent that runs an expand / backfill / contract migration on a live Postgres table. When another session holds the rows it needs, it rolls back the chunk, records who holds the lock, shrinks its batch, waits, and resumes from a saved cursor. It will not prepare the destructive step until a deterministic verifier proves parity, and it will not run that step until an owner approves the exact SQL.

**Demo:** [179-second execution UI recording](https://github.com/Sher110106/migration-parachute/releases/download/v0.1.0/execution-ui-replay.mp4) · [release notes](https://github.com/Sher110106/migration-parachute/releases/tag/v0.1.0)

Built for neatHack 2026 (10–12 October 2026). All code in this repository was written during the event.

> The demo runs on a **fictional local fixture**: 2,000 customers and 10,000 orders on local Postgres 15, emails on the reserved `.test` domain. It never touches a real database.

## Results

Same fixture, same seeded fault: a separate session holds row locks on keys 4,001–4,100 for 6 seconds while the backfill reaches them. The per-statement lock budget is 300 ms.

| Run | Outcome | Retries | Lock wait | Rows kept |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Baseline: one `UPDATE` in one transaction | `FAILED`, whole transaction rolled back | – | 452 ms | 0 |
| Agent with first recovery policy (`naive-retry/v0`: same batch, 50 ms wait) | `PAUSED_LOCK_BUDGET`, retry budget spent | 6 | 2,647 ms | 4,000 |
| Agent with fixed recovery policy (`adaptive/v1`) | parity proven, `CONTRACT_READY` | 4 | 1,817 ms | 10,000 |

| Agent with a language-model planner (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash via OpenRouter, inside the same policy fence) | parity proven, `CONTRACT_READY` | 2 | 751 ms | 10,000 |

Neither failing run claims success. Full replay suite, 12 scenarios: v0 passes 11, v1 passes 12. Both have zero false successes and zero destructive statements run without approval. Raw records: [`evidence/replay-naive-v0.json`](evidence/replay-naive-v0.json) and [`evidence/replay-adaptive-v1.json`](evidence/replay-adaptive-v1.json). Lock-wait figures vary by tens of milliseconds between runs; three repeats of each policy gave the same outcome every time.

The language-model planner passes all 12 scenarios with no rejected decisions: 14 decisions, 9,278 input and 5,239 output tokens, $0.0094 in total ([`evidence/replay-llm-deepseek-v4.1-flash.json`](evidence/replay-llm-deepseek-v4.1-flash.json)). On the lock run it read the blocker's age from the error evidence: after the first timeout it waited 1 s; when the blocking transaction was 4.1 s old it waited 3 s, so it needed two retries where the fixed policy needed four. Each answer must name one of the actions policy allows, inside its bounds; anything else is rejected and recorded, and the deterministic planner answers instead.

The v0 policy was committed and measured before the fix. The git history shows the order: `ed9edbe` (v0, 11/12) then `5e05e92` (fix, 12/12). The records each commit produced at the time are kept in [`evidence/history/`](evidence/history/); they used a 3.0 s lock. The lock is now held for 6 s, because v1's blocker inspection made each failed attempt slower, and at 3.5 s the naive policy sometimes outlasted the lock.

## What the agent does

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  spec[MigrationSpec] --> orch[Orchestrator]
  orch -->|observation + allowed options| planner[Planner: Claude or deterministic]
  planner -->|one action| guard[Policy guard]
  guard -->|typed tool call| pg[(Postgres)]
  pg --> verify[Deterministic verifier]
  orch <--> store[(Event log + checkpoints)]
  orch --> traces[neatlogs traces]
  verify --> gate{Owner approval}
  gate -->|approved SQL hash| contract[Contract]
```

1. **Inspect** the table and reject a bad spec before any side effect: non-unique key, ambiguous lookup, wrong database, or a column that someone else already owns.
2. **Plan** expand, backfill and contract SQL from a typed change. The planner never writes SQL.
3. **Expand**: add a nullable column and a dual-write trigger, and build the index concurrently. Each step writes an idempotency ledger row in the same transaction.
4. **Backfill** in key-range chunks, one short transaction each, with a lock timeout. On failure, ask the planner for one action from the options policy allows (retry with a batch size and wait inside set bounds, pause, or abort). Anything outside those bounds is rejected and recorded.
5. **Verify** in one consistent snapshot: parity checksum, null targets, mismatches, orphans, pending ranges, index validity. If new rows arrived, run a catch-up pass first.
6. **Guard the contract**: fresh proof, no views or functions still reading the old column, then prepare the SQL and an approval ID bound to the SQL hash and proof hash.
7. **Wait for approval.** Only then add the foreign key, set NOT NULL, drop the trigger and drop the old column, and verify the result.

Every step appends to a hash-chained event log. A pure reducer rebuilds run state from it. Appends use compare-and-swap on the revision and a fencing token, and a Postgres advisory lock allows one worker per run. After a crash, a new worker adopts chunks the database committed but the control store never recorded, by reading the ledger. Nothing is re-run blindly.

## Scenarios

| Scenario | Expected behaviour |
|---|---|
| `clean` | Expand, backfill, verify; stop at the approval gate |
| `clean_approved` | Same, then the owner approves; contract runs and verifies |
| `baseline_lock_timeout` | One-transaction backfill fails under the lock; no success claimed |
| `lock_timeout` | Roll back, record blocker, shrink batch, back off, resume from the same cursor |
| `crash_after_commit` | Worker dies after the database commits a chunk; a new worker adopts it from the ledger |
| `parity_mismatch` | A writer bypasses the trigger; verifier blocks the contract |
| `schema_drift` | Unrelated column added after planning; re-inspect and replan |
| `schema_conflict` | Target column exists with the wrong type; fail before expand |
| `concurrent_inserts` | Rows arrive mid-backfill, some skipping triggers; catch-up pass |
| `invalid_key` | Non-unique chunk key; reject with no side effects |
| `budget` | Cost cap reached; pause with the checkpoint, resume with a higher cap |
| `view_dependency` | A view still reads the old column; contract paused for the operator |

## Partner tools

- **neatlogs** traces every run as one `WORKFLOW` with nested `AGENT` (planner decisions), `TOOL` (database calls, lock inspection, ledger reconciliation), `GUARDRAIL` (spec validation, drift, contract guard, fail-closed) and `EVALUATOR` (expand, backfill and contract verification) spans. Attributes carry hashes, counts, SQLSTATEs and timings, never row values. The same tree is written locally to `var/traces/` for the UI. The before/after runs were exported to neatlogs; their trace ids are in [`evidence/neatlogs-before-naive-v0.json`](evidence/neatlogs-before-naive-v0.json) and [`evidence/neatlogs-after-adaptive-v1.json`](evidence/neatlogs-after-adaptive-v1.json), with public companion screenshots [`evidence/neatlogs-before.png`](evidence/neatlogs-before.png) and [`evidence/neatlogs-after.png`](evidence/neatlogs-after.png). Each process initialises neatlogs once, and every trace of one run shares the run id as its session.
- **Entire** records the coding-agent sessions that built this repository. Each commit carries an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer; `entire checkpoint explain <id>` shows the prompts and decisions behind it, including the v0-to-v1 recovery fix.
- **cfo.ai** holds the business model: price, runs per customer, the measured cost ledger per run, and three adoption scenarios. See [`docs/cfo-model-inputs.md`](docs/cfo-model-inputs.md), the [independent verification](evidence/cfo/model-verification.md), and the [Migration Parachute business-plan page](https://app.cfo.ai/sher-cfoai-a1e2b615/pages/a8fa343a-4234-4a54-a784-971b110829a8).

## AI tools used

Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote most of the code under the author's direction. Entire captured those sessions as checkpoints. Earlier planning used OpenAI Codex. The research and architecture notes were written before kickoff, as the rules allow; they are not part of this repository.

## Limits

- One change kind so far: replace a text column with a foreign key found by lookup.
- Integer primary keys only, because backfill chunks by key range.
- The fixture, faults and evidence are local. No production database has been tested.
- The contract assumes the application has stopped writing the old column; the owner confirms that when approving.

## Layout

```
src/parachute/
  domain.py        typed contracts and events
  state.py         pure reducer
  store.py         SQLite event log, checkpoints, fencing
  pg.py            Postgres adapter with idempotency ledger
  sqlgen.py        SQL generated from the typed change
  orchestrator.py  the agent loop
```
